cards.title: Same prompts, two sizes
cards.body: The lab feeds ten identical prompts to the pre-trained (not instruction-tuned) Gemma-1B and Gemma-4B, using greedy decoding and 50 new tokens each, and times each loop. With every setting held fixed, the differences come from model size alone.

cards.title: Bigger: better but slower
cards.body: Gemma-4B usually recalls facts more accurately and writes more nuanced text, for instance on the proverb "A roaring lion kills no game", where wild coffee originated, and the world's deepest river. But it takes considerably longer to generate.

cards.title: Choose for the task
cards.body: There is no single best model. Prefer a larger one when quality, accuracy and detail are paramount; prefer a smaller one when speed matters and good-enough answers are acceptable, as in a real-time chatbot. It is always a balance between needs and resources.

cards.title: The generation loop
cards.body: Each loop is timed with time.time_ns(), which returns nanoseconds; dividing by 1,000,000,000 gives seconds. Before loading Gemma-4B, the lab deletes Gemma-1B with del to free GPU memory.
cards.code:
for p in list_of_prompts:
    out, logits, tok = (
        generation.prompt_transformer_model(
            p, max_new_tokens=50,
            loaded_model=gemma_1b_model,
            sampling_mode="greedy"))
    generations_gemma_1b.append(out)

exercises.prompt: Which model generated its ten answers faster?
exercises.explain: Fewer parameters mean less computation per token, so the 1B model finishes the loop sooner.

exercises.prompt: Which prompt does the lab cite as one where Gemma-4B did better?
options: The national flower of South Africa is
The tallest mountain in Africa is
The Maasai ethnic group originate from
What 'A roaring lion kills no game' means
exercises.explain: The lab highlights the proverb, the origin of wild coffee and the world's deepest river as cases where Gemma-4B was more accurate or nuanced.

exercises.prompt: Gemma-4B tended to give more factually accurate answers than Gemma-1B.
exercises.explain: Its larger parameter count lets it store and recall more facts, at the cost of slower generation.

exercises.prompt: Running both models on the same prompts with the same decoding settings makes the comparison fair.
exercises.explain: Holding prompts, token budget and greedy decoding fixed isolates model size as the one thing that differs.

exercises.prompt: Before loading Gemma-4B, the lab runs `___ gemma_1b_model` to free memory.
exercises.explain: Python's del removes the reference to the 1B model, so its GPU memory can be reclaimed for the larger model.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the divisor that turns nanoseconds into seconds.
exercises.code:
before_loop = time.time_ns()
# ... generate for every prompt ...
after_loop = time.time_ns()
duration_ns = after_loop - before_loop
total_seconds = duration_ns / ___
exercises.explain: One second is 10⁹ nanoseconds, so dividing the time.time_ns() difference by 1,000,000,000 gives seconds.

exercises.prompt: The lab prints whole minutes ("minute" when 1) and seconds to 2 decimals. What does it show here?
exercises.explain: 95 // 60 = 1 whole minute and 95 % 60 = 35 seconds; because minutes equals 1, the singular "minute" is used.

exercises.prompt: Why does the lab use greedy decoding for both models?
options: To remove sampling randomness from the test
Because greedy decoding saves GPU memory
Because it makes the larger model faster
exercises.explain: Greedy decoding is deterministic, so differences between the outputs reflect the models rather than luck in sampling.

exercises.prompt: Order the lab's steps.
items: Time Gemma-1B on the ten prompts
Time Gemma-4B on the same prompts
Compare speed and quality side by side
exercises.explain: Each model is loaded and timed in turn, with the 1B model removed first so the 4B one fits; then the outputs are compared.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its description.
pairs: Takes the most likely token every step
Caps how many tokens are generated
exercises.explain: The lab compares two Gemma sizes under fixed decoding settings and measures elapsed time in nanoseconds.

exercises.prompt: Your app must reply instantly on modest hardware, and approximate answers are fine. Which fits the lab's takeaway?
options: Gemma-4B, since bigger is always better
Either; size does not affect speed
Gemma-4B, since it needs less memory
exercises.explain: When latency and resources matter more than top accuracy, the smaller model is the sensible trade-off.

exercises.prompt: The best model is always the largest one you can afford to run.
exercises.explain: The lab stresses that the right choice depends on the task: a larger model's quality must be weighed against its speed and cost.

exercises.prompt: Larger models usually trade ___ for quality.
exercises.explain: Gemma-4B gave higher-quality text but took considerably longer than Gemma-1B to generate it.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of Gemma models does this lab compare?
exercises.explain: The lab uses the original pre-trained Gemma-1B and Gemma-4B, not variants instruction-tuned for dialogue.

cards.title: FLOPs vs FLOPS
cards.body: A FLOP is one floating-point operation, such as a multiply or an add. FLOPs (small s) counts the total work for a job; FLOPS (capital S) is a speed, operations per second. A job of 1,000 FLOPs on hardware running at 100 FLOPS takes 10 seconds.

cards.title: The 6·P·N rule
cards.body: For one epoch, FLOPs ≈ 6 × P × N, with P trainable parameters and N training tokens. The forward pass costs about 2PN (a multiply and an add per parameter per token); the backward pass about 4PN, roughly twice the forward.

cards.title: Why estimate first?
cards.body: A FLOPs estimate made before training tells you roughly what it will cost, whether your hardware can handle it, and how long it may take: divide the FLOPs by the hardware's FLOPS.

cards.title: Real-world scale
cards.body: BERT-base (110M params, 3.3B tokens) ≈ 2.18e18 FLOPs. T5-large (770M, 1T) ≈ 4.62e21. Gemma-1B on Africa Galore (1B, 30K) ≈ 1.8e14. PaLM (540B, 780B) ≈ 2.53e24. Cost is linear in P and in N, so 10× either one means 10× the FLOPs.

exercises.prompt: What does FLOPS, with a capital S, measure?
options: Total operations needed to train a model
Bytes of memory a GPU can hold
Operations a device performs per second
Tokens a model processes per epoch
exercises.explain: The capital S means "per second": FLOPS is a speed. FLOPs with a small s is a total count of operations.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the factor in the lab's FLOPs estimate for one epoch.
exercises.explain: FLOPs ≈ 6 × P × N: about 2PN for the forward pass plus about 4PN for the backward pass.

exercises.prompt: Why is the backward pass estimated at about 4 × P × N FLOPs?
options: It repeats the forward pass four times
Computing gradients costs about twice the forward pass
It updates four optimizer states per weight
Each weight is read from memory four times
exercises.explain: Backpropagation computes gradients for both activations and weights, roughly double the forward pass's 2PN.

exercises.prompt: Estimate the FLOPs to train a 1-billion-parameter model on 20 billion tokens for one epoch.
Gemma-1B on Africa Galore needs about 1.8e14 FLOPs. On hardware sustaining 1e14 FLOPS, roughly how long is that?
exercises.explain: Time = FLOPs ÷ FLOPS = 1.8e14 ÷ 1e14 = 1.8 seconds, ignoring real-world inefficiencies.

exercises.prompt: A 70-billion-parameter model trains on 1.5 trillion tokens. About how many FLOPs is one epoch?
exercises.explain: 6 × 7e10 × 1.5e12 = 63e22 = 6.3e23. Forgetting the factor 6 would give 1.05e23.

exercises.prompt: Doubling the number of training tokens roughly doubles the estimated FLOPs.
exercises.explain: FLOPs ≈ 6PN is linear in N, so twice the tokens means twice the compute.

exercises.prompt: A GPU rated at 200 TeraFLOPS can perform 200 trillion operations in total over its lifetime.
exercises.explain: TeraFLOPS is a rate: 200 trillion floating-point operations every second.

exercises.prompt: The forward pass costs about ___ × P × N FLOPs: one multiply and one add per parameter per token.
exercises.explain: Each parameter takes part in a multiply-accumulate, that is two operations, for every token.

exercises.prompt: Match each symbol or term to its meaning.
pairs: Number of tokens in the training set
exercises.explain: Adding the forward (2PN) and backward (4PN) costs gives the 6PN rule for one epoch.

exercises.prompt: Order these training runs from fewest to most FLOPs.
exercises.explain: 6PN gives about 1.8e14, 2.2e18, 4.6e21 and 2.5e24 FLOPs respectively.

exercises.prompt: On the lab's log-scale sliders, moving log_param_count from 9 to 10 does what to FLOPs?
exercises.explain: Each slider step is a factor of 10 in parameters, and FLOPs grow linearly with P, so they grow 10×.

exercises.prompt: In Python scientific notation, 2.5 billion is written ___.
exercises.explain: e9 means × 10⁹, a billion, so 2.5e9 = 2,500,000,000.

exercises.prompt: In FLOPs ≈ 6 × P × N for one epoch, what is N?
options: Total tokens in the training dataset
exercises.explain: N counts tokens, not examples or epochs: each token goes through one forward and one backward pass per epoch.

exercises.prompt: Training for 3 epochs would take roughly 18 × P × N FLOPs.
exercises.explain: 6PN is the cost of one pass over the data; three passes cost about three times as much, 18PN.

cards.title: The plan: Gemma-4B
cards.body: In course 5, LoRA made fine-tuning Gemma-1B possible on a T4 GPU. The obvious next step is the same recipe on the 4-billion-parameter Gemma-4B, the model that gave better answers in the size-comparison lab.

cards.title: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
cards.body: Loading the gemma3_4b_text preset with default 32-bit floats fails before training even starts. RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED is the GPU's out-of-memory (OOM) error, and the message says how much memory it tried to allocate.
cards.code:
model = keras_hub.models.Gemma3CausalLM\
    .from_preset(preset="gemma3_4b_text")
# RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: out of memory

cards.title: LoRA can't help here
cards.body: LoRA shrinks what you train, not what you store: all 4 billion frozen weights must still sit in GPU memory. At 4 bytes each that is 16 billion bytes, about 14.9 GB, which is essentially the whole T4 before any data, activations or gradients.

cards.title: Getting past the wall
cards.body: Memory is the bottleneck, and it can be attacked: store numbers in fewer bits (bfloat16), train fewer parameters (LoRA), and keep real batches small while simulating big ones (gradient accumulation). The size-comparison lab quietly used such tricks to load Gemma-4B.

exercises.prompt: What does a RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED error from the GPU mean?
options: The GPU ran out of memory
exercises.explain: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED is the technical name for an out-of-memory (OOM) error; it also reports how much it tried to allocate.

exercises.prompt: When did the attempt to use Gemma-4B in 32-bit precision fail?
exercises.explain: It failed before training began: the 32-bit weights alone did not fit in the GPU's memory.

exercises.prompt: How many bytes do 4 billion parameters take in 32-bit floats?
exercises.explain: 32 bits = 4 bytes, so 4e9 × 4 = 16e9 bytes, about 14.9 GB in 1024-based units.

exercises.prompt: LoRA reduces the memory needed to hold the frozen pre-trained weights.
exercises.explain: LoRA cuts what you train, not what you store: every frozen weight must still be loaded onto the GPU.

exercises.prompt: The size-comparison lab could load Gemma-4B because it quietly used memory-saving techniques.
exercises.explain: This lab notes that the earlier loader already applied efficiency techniques in the background.

exercises.prompt: In 32-bit floating point, each parameter takes ___ bytes.
exercises.explain: A byte is 8 bits, so 32 bits = 4 bytes per number.

exercises.prompt: Which memory costs does LoRA actually shrink?
options: The input batch of token IDs
exercises.explain: Training extras are needed only for trainable weights, and with LoRA those are just the small low-rank matrices.

exercises.prompt: A T4 has about 15 GB and JAX may use 90% of it. Gemma-4B's 32-bit weights need ~14.9 GB. Can it load?
options: Yes: 14.9 GB is just under 15 GB
No: weights exceed the ~13.5 GB usable
Yes: LoRA keeps most weights off the GPU
No: the tokenizer alone is too big
exercises.explain: 0.9 × 15 GB ≈ 13.5 GB, less than the 14.9 GB of weights, and inputs and activations would need more on top.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens in this lab.
items: Reflect on what fills GPU memory
exercises.explain: Data preparation succeeds; the run stops at model loading with an OOM, which motivates studying where memory goes.

exercises.prompt: Match each technique to how it saves memory.
pairs: Halves the bytes per stored number
Shrinks the set of trainable weights
Large effective batch from small batches
Fewer weights to store in the first place
exercises.explain: These are the levers for getting past the memory wall on a single T4 GPU.

exercises.prompt: Why do bigger models hit the memory wall first?
options: Bigger models must train for more epochs
Weight memory grows with parameter count
exercises.explain: Weight memory is parameters × bytes each, so a 4B model needs four times the memory of a 1B model.

exercises.prompt: An OOM while loading means the model's ___ alone don't fit.
exercises.explain: At load time nothing is being trained, so no gradients or optimizer states exist yet; only the weights are being placed in memory.

exercises.prompt: Storing Gemma-4B in 16-bit numbers instead would cut its weights to about 8 billion bytes.
exercises.explain: 16 bits = 2 bytes, so 4e9 × 2 = 8e9 bytes (≈7.45 GB), half the 32-bit size. This is the idea behind bfloat16.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the preset that loads the text-only Gemma-4B.
exercises.explain: "gemma3_4b_text" is the Keras Hub preset for Gemma-4B; "gemma3_1b" was the smaller model from course 5.

cards.title: Five things on the GPU
cards.body: Training must fit five things in GPU memory: model parameters, the input batch and activations, which inference needs too, plus gradients and optimizer states, which only training needs. If their sum exceeds the GPU's capacity, you get an out-of-memory error.

cards.title: Per-parameter costs
cards.body: Gradients store one number per parameter, and Adam keeps two states per parameter. So training needs at least 4× the bytes of the weights alone. Input memory is just token IDs.
cards.code:
params = P * bytes_per_param
grads = P * bytes_per_param
adam = 2 * P * bytes_per_param
inputs = batch * max_len * bytes_per_id

cards.title: Activations
cards.body: Each layer outputs an embedding-sized vector per token, and training keeps every layer's output for the backward pass: batch × length × layers × embedding dim × bytes. For the lab's Gemma-4B setup that is 8 × 1024 × 32 × 2560 × 4 bytes = 2.5 GB.

cards.title: The verdict for Gemma-4B
cards.body: In float32 (1 GB = 1024³ bytes): parameters 14.90, gradients 14.90, Adam 29.80, activations 2.50, inputs ≈0. Inference ≈ 17.4 GB; training ≈ 62.1 GB, far above a ~16 GB GPU. bfloat16 (2 bytes) halves everything: ≈ 8.7 and ≈ 31.05 GB.

exercises.prompt: Which two memory components are needed only during training?
exercises.explain: Inference needs parameters, inputs and activations; training adds a gradient per parameter and the optimizer's states.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the factor for Adam's optimizer states.
exercises.explain: Adam stores two values per parameter, so its memory is 2 × parameters × bytes per parameter.

exercises.prompt: Activations: batch 8, length 1024, 32 layers, embedding 2560, 4 bytes each. About how much memory? (1 GB = 1024³ bytes)
exercises.explain: 8 × 1024 × 32 × 2560 × 4 = 2,684,354,560 bytes, exactly 2.5 GB. Leaving out the batch gives 0.31; leaving out layers gives 0.08.

exercises.prompt: How much memory do 1 billion float32 parameters take? (1 GB = 1024³ bytes)
Gemma-4B in bfloat16 (2 bytes per number): how much memory do Adam's optimizer states need?
exercises.explain: 2 states × 4e9 parameters × 2 bytes = 16e9 bytes ≈ 14.9 GB, the biggest single item even in bfloat16.

exercises.prompt: Running inference requires memory for gradients too.
exercises.explain: Gradients are only computed to update weights. Inference needs parameters, inputs and activations.

exercises.prompt: Changing every component from 4 to 2 bytes per number halves the total estimate.
exercises.explain: Each formula is linear in the bytes per number, so halving it halves every component and the total.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the missing factor of the activation-memory formula.
exercises.explain: Activations are kept for every layer for the backward pass, so the per-sequence cost is multiplied by the number of layers.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the last factor of the input-batch memory.
exercises.explain: The input batch is just token IDs: batch × length of them, each taking bytes_per_token_id bytes.

exercises.prompt: Why are every layer's activations kept during training?
options: They are reused as inputs for the next batch
The optimizer stores them as its two states
They speed up loading the model's weights
The backward pass needs them for gradients
exercises.explain: Backpropagation works back through each layer and needs that layer's stored forward-pass outputs.

exercises.prompt: Total float32 memory to fine-tune all of Gemma-4B in the lab's setup is about:
exercises.explain: 14.90 (params) + 14.90 (grads) + 29.80 (Adam) + 2.50 (activations) + ~0 (inputs) ≈ 62.1 GB. 17.4 GB is inference only.

exercises.prompt: Match each component to its memory formula.
pairs: P × bytes, needed even for inference
batch × length × bytes per token ID
exercises.explain: Three components scale with the parameter count; inputs and activations scale with batch size and sequence length.

exercises.prompt: Rank these Gemma-4B float32 components from largest to smallest.
exercises.explain: Adam ≈ 29.8 GB, parameters ≈ 14.9 GB, activations 2.5 GB, and the input IDs only about 0.00003 GB.

exercises.prompt: How does the lab's bytes_to_gb convert bytes to gigabytes?
exercises.explain: It returns num_bytes / (1024**3), so 1 GB here means 1,073,741,824 bytes.

exercises.prompt: With bfloat16, Gemma-4B inference (~8.7 GB) fits on a 16 GB GPU, but full training (~31 GB) still does not.
exercises.explain: Halving the bytes makes inference fit, but full training still needs about twice the GPU, hence LoRA and other tricks.

cards.title: One argument to load it
cards.body: bfloat16 stores each number in 16 bits (2 bytes) instead of 32, halving the memory for weights. That single change lets Gemma-4B load on a T4. Printing a layer's kernel dtype, such as the query projection in decoder_block_0, confirms the format.

cards.title: Still need LoRA
cards.body: Even in bfloat16, full fine-tuning won't fit. With rank-4 LoRA enabled, gradients and optimizer states are needed only for the small low-rank matrices, so the 4B model trains on one T4 at batch size 1.

cards.title: Stable low-precision training
cards.body: Less precise numbers make training touchier, so the lab uses settings found to be stable: AdamW with a small learning rate, light weight decay, beta_2 of 0.95, and clipnorm 0.5 to cap gradient size. It trains for 4 epochs.
cards.code:
optimizer = keras.optimizers.AdamW(
    learning_rate=5e-5,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.95,
    epsilon=1e-6,
    clipnorm=0.5,
)

cards.title: Watching the epochs
cards.body: Three probes: Kente cloth (in the data), Kilimanjaro without "Mount" (generalization), and Tokyo (absent from the data, so pre-trained knowledge). Epoch 1 was unstable, with a looping "KMnO4" token and repeated "Category:" lists, but by epoch 4 the answers were fluent, factual and well formatted.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the dtype that halves the memory for Gemma-4B's weights.
exercises.explain: Passing dtype="bfloat16" loads every parameter as a 16-bit number instead of the default 32-bit float.

exercises.prompt: How much storage does bfloat16 use per number?
exercises.explain: The 16 in bfloat16 is its bit width: 2 bytes, half of float32's 4.

exercises.prompt: How many bytes do Gemma-4B's 4 billion weights need in bfloat16?
exercises.explain: 4e9 × 2 bytes = 8e9 bytes, about 7.45 GB: half the 16 billion bytes needed in float32.

exercises.prompt: Why enable LoRA even after switching to bfloat16?
options: bfloat16 weights can only be updated through LoRA layers
LoRA converts the weights back to float32
LoRA is needed to read turn delimiters
Full training's gradients and Adam states won't fit
exercises.explain: bfloat16 makes the weights fit, but training every parameter would add a gradient and two Adam states per weight, far too much.

exercises.prompt: The lab's final generations showed that bfloat16 badly hurt answer quality.
exercises.explain: By epoch 4 the answers were high-quality, factual and correctly formatted, so bfloat16 did not noticeably harm the result.

exercises.prompt: Training in low precision can be more sensitive, so stable optimizer settings matter.
exercises.explain: With less precise numbers the learning process is touchier, which is why the lab picks conservative AdamW settings.

exercises.prompt: In the lab's AdamW setup, what does clipnorm=0.5 do?
options: Freezes half of the model's parameters
Caps the gradient's size to keep updates stable
Halves the learning rate after each epoch
exercises.explain: Gradient clipping rescales any gradient whose norm exceeds 0.5, preventing sudden large updates during sensitive bfloat16 training.

exercises.prompt: Which test prompt checks that pre-trained knowledge survives fine-tuning?
exercises.explain: Nothing about Tokyo or Japan is in the fine-tuning data, so a good answer must come from what Gemma learned in pre-training.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the attribute that reveals the weights' number format.
exercises.explain: The dtype attribute reports the data type; after loading with dtype="bfloat16" it prints bfloat16.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to what it shows or tests.
exercises.explain: The probes separate fine-tuning knowledge, generalization and retained pre-training; epochs 1 and 4 show the arc from unstable to polished.

exercises.prompt: Order the lab's steps.
items: Compile with a stable AdamW setup
exercises.explain: The model must load in bfloat16 before LoRA is added, and the optimizer is compiled before fit runs with the per-epoch monitor.

exercises.prompt: Would Gemma-27B's weights fit on a ~16 GB T4 in bfloat16?
options: Yes: bfloat16 brings them down to ~13.5 GB
Yes: LoRA keeps them off the GPU
No: bfloat16 only works up to 4B
No: they'd need about 54 billion bytes
exercises.explain: 27e9 × 2 bytes = 54e9 bytes ≈ 50 GB, several times a T4's memory, even before any training extras.

exercises.prompt: With LoRA on, gradients and optimizer states are kept only for the ___ matrices.
exercises.explain: Only the small LoRA matrices are trainable, so only they need gradients and Adam states.

exercises.prompt: Loading Gemma-4B successfully needed only one change from the failed attempt: the dtype.
exercises.explain: The failed lab used default 32-bit floats; adding dtype="bfloat16" was the single change that made loading, and LoRA fine-tuning, possible.

exercises.prompt: When does the GenerationMonitor callback print its outputs?
options: At the end of every epoch
exercises.explain: Its on_epoch_end method runs after each epoch and prints generations for the three test prompts.

cards.title: Why bigger batches?
cards.body: Averaging gradients over more examples gives less noisy, more stable updates, and a GPU processes a bigger batch in parallel more efficiently. The catch: activation memory grows with batch size, so going from 1 to 4 means roughly 4× the activations.

cards.title: The batch-size-4 OOM
cards.body: With Gemma-4B in bfloat16 plus LoRA, batch_size=4 fails with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: the GPU could not find another 52,428,800 bytes (about 52 MB). Batch size 1 fits. After an OOM, restarting the Colab session is the surest way to free GPU memory.

cards.title: Accumulate, then update
cards.body: Gradient accumulation runs forward and backward passes on several small batches, adds up their gradients, and updates the weights only after a set number of steps. Effective batch size = physical batch × accumulation steps, so 1 × 8 behaves like a batch of 8.

cards.title: In Keras
cards.body: The learning rate is scaled 8× to match the 8× effective batch, while fit keeps batch_size=1. Compared with the plain batch-1 run, outputs became coherent sooner, with no KMnO4 loops and a lower final loss.
cards.code:
optimizer = keras.optimizers.AdamW(
    learning_rate=8e-4,  # 8 × 1e-4
    weight_decay=0.01,
    # betas and epsilon as before
    clipnorm=0.5,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
)

exercises.prompt: The physical batch size is 1. Fill in the value that simulates a batch of 8.
exercises.code:
optimizer = keras.optimizers.AdamW(
    learning_rate=8e-4,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    clipnorm=0.5,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=___,
)
exercises.explain: Effective batch = physical batch × steps, so 1 × 8 = 8: the optimizer updates after summing 8 batches' gradients.

exercises.prompt: Physical batch size 2 with gradient_accumulation_steps=4. What is the effective batch size?
exercises.explain: Effective batch = 2 × 4, so 8 examples contribute to each weight update.

exercises.prompt: You want an effective batch of 32, but only batches of 4 fit. How many accumulation steps?
exercises.explain: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 small batches must be accumulated before each update.

exercises.prompt: Why did batch_size=4 run out of memory when batch_size=1 worked?
options: The model's weights were copied four times
The optimizer kept four states per weight
Activation memory grew about 4× with the batch
exercises.explain: Weights and optimizer states don't depend on batch size, but activations are stored per example, so 4 examples need about 4× the activations.

exercises.prompt: With gradient accumulation, the weights are updated after every small batch.
exercises.explain: Gradients from each small batch are summed, and the optimizer updates the weights only once the set number of steps is reached.

exercises.prompt: Gradient accumulation gives a large-batch learning signal without large-batch activation memory.
exercises.explain: Only one small batch's activations are in memory at a time, yet each update reflects many examples.

exercises.prompt: Base lr is 1e-4 at batch 1. Following the lab's scaling, which lr goes with gradient_accumulation_steps=4?
exercises.explain: The lab scales the learning rate with the effective batch: 1e-4 × 4 = 4e-4, just as it used 8 × 1e-4 = 8e-4 for 8 steps.

exercises.prompt: The OOM message said it tried to allocate 52428800 bytes. Roughly how much is that?
exercises.explain: 52,428,800 bytes is about 52 million bytes, roughly 52 MB (exactly 50 MiB): a small extra amount that still did not fit.

exercises.prompt: Order one gradient-accumulation cycle.
items: Forward pass on a small batch
Backward pass to get its gradients
Add them to the running gradient sum
Repeat until the step count is reached
Update weights with the combined gradient
exercises.explain: Each small batch adds its gradients to a running sum; only after the last step does the optimizer apply one update.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The GPU is out of memory
Clears variables and frees GPU memory
exercises.explain: Accumulation separates what fits in memory (the physical batch) from what the optimizer sees per update (the effective batch).

exercises.prompt: Compared with the batch-1 bfloat16 run, what did gradient accumulation produce?
options: Faster epochs but worse final answers
Coherent outputs sooner and a lower final loss
Identical outputs at every single epoch
An OOM error at the very first update
exercises.explain: The lab saw fluent, factual outputs by epoch 2, no KMnO4 loops, and a lower final loss with higher accuracy.

exercises.prompt: Raising the batch size mostly increases ___ memory.
exercises.explain: Parameters and optimizer states depend on model size; activations are stored per example, so they scale with batch size.

exercises.prompt: With 8 accumulation steps, what physical batch size does the lab pass to fit?
exercises.code:
history = model.fit(
    data,
    epochs=num_epochs,
